notes: \cpara{Traces the physical chain from sunlight to your belief that your shoelaces are untied.}
\cpara{Claims the key to deliberate reasoning is that this process is understandable, so you can ask which ways of thinking produce accurate beliefs.}
\cpara{Contrasts mice, which see without understanding seeing, with humans, who can, and invites the reader to marvel at it.}
\cpara{Explains that humans, unlike mice, can recognize flaws in their own perception, such as optical illusions, by keeping the senses distinct from reality.}
\cpara{Describes science as reasoning about which process makes beliefs match the world, understandable and useful outside the laboratory.}

\cpara{Repeats the two paragraphs before it: the mice again, the wonder again. The one new claim, that the power belongs to ``individuals, not just scientific societies,'' is the essay's real thesis. It sits in a trailing clause, with no argument, after a dash.}

\cpara{The premise the whole essay needs, that a mind can be understood and corrected as a machine can, stated in one sentence and defended with a joke. The italics do the arguing. ``A little more complicated'' is irony, and irony is not a reason.}

\cpara{The essay's only case, and it is thin. One anonymous person, in an undated chat, as the author recalls it. The question itself is lopsided: ``If no, why not?'' demands reasons only from people who expect no war. The author's survey applies scrutiny to one answer only, which is the fault the essay goes on to describe.}

\cpara{The diagnosis is mind-reading. From two words the author infers the man's unhappiness and a causal story about his brain. Then the parallel worlds arrive to say something ordinary probability says without them: optimism does not predict peace. The rest is decoration.}

\clogic{The same device as in ``The Bottom Line,'' with the same Tegmark footnote. A frequency over many similar cases does all the work. Contested physics is brought in to make an everyday point sound like a technical result.}

\cpara{The principle, in two sentences: what you would like to be true is not evidence. It is correct and entirely familiar; ``wishful thinking'' names it. The paragraph adds jargon (``entangled'') and one more metaphor for the mind.}

\cpara{The conclusion promises a ``reflective correction'' and never says what it is, how large it should be, or how to know it worked. ``In practice'' claims results; the essay reports none. The author had already written the opposite warning. In ``Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People,'' posted in April 2007, five months earlier: ``If you're irrational to start with, having more knowledge can hurt you.'' The conclusion drops that warning and sells the knowledge as power.}
\clogic{``Far more powerful'' is the essay's largest claim, and it comes with no evidence.}
\cpara{Cites Max Tegmark's essay on parallel universes, the source of the ``Tegmark duplicates'' in the text.}

\cpara{The footnote holds the essay's only quantitative idea: a small effect should shift belief by a small amount. That idea is the whole answer to the question of how large a correction should be, and it is in a footnote.}
\clogic{The essay says it must now measure, and then measures nothing. No number enters Bayes's theorem.}
